Our findings provide limited evidence that source cues matter for credibility judgments in social media nutrition posts. In the topic-specific regressions, the differences between expert and influencer posts are generally small and not robust across models. However, when responses are pooled across both red meat and seed oil claims in our within-subjects design, influencer posts are rated as less credible (p < .05), suggesting a modest overall source cue effect. These findings suggest that any source effect is likely small and context-dependent. Prior beliefs also appear to play a notable role, suggesting that source cues are interpreted through respondents' existing attitudes to expertise and health information.

Despite our findings, we still have unresolved questions. Measuring credibility is a tough task, and there are surely more covariates that affect an individual's beliefs. We attempted to capture some of this by measuring baseline indices, but these likely tipped participants off about the focus of our survey. We also built very simple versions of these indices by just adding up response values into a cumulative number, but more thought is warranted to better measure prior beliefs. The randomization order effect from which nutrition claim we show first is puzzling and could be a subject of a whole new experiment in its own right. As mentioned, it may indicate the topic-dependent nature of credibility judgments. With more power, we would test source cues across a greater number of topics. We also debated internally if our focus on source cues and authenticity is sufficient to capture how people make decisions about credibility given the increasing questioning of the credibility of online posts related to algorithms, politicization, and AI use.
